The rule sets explicit limits around the rolling mean of the log price spread, two standard deviations above and two standard deviations below the 130-day moving average, and a position is opened only when the spread moves outside one of those bands. An unbounded rule would have the strategy trading on every small fluctuation in the spread, which is the opposite of a mean-reversion design: the bands exist precisely to separate a divergence large enough to be worth betting on from ordinary noise. Exit is bounded in the same way, at the moving average itself.

questions.stem: A pairs trade is opened when the spread between two correlated stocks moves more than two standard deviations from its moving average and closed when the spread returns to that average. Over a multi-year sample, this rule is most likely to produce:

options.A: no entry signals at all.
options.B: gains on some trades and a loss after a structural break.
options.C: gains on every trade.

rationales.A: The rule does generate entries. Applied to the Canadian National Railway (CNR) and Canadian Pacific Railway (CP) pair, it produced three trades over the 2014-2016 sample. The first was opened on 2 October 2014, when the spread crossed the -2 standard deviation mark, the position being long CNR and short CP, and was closed on 18 November 2014, when the spread reached the moving average; it was profitable and was held for slightly more than a month. A two standard deviation band on a 130-day rolling window is wide enough to keep the strategy out of ordinary noise but is crossed several times over a sample of this length, which is what makes the strategy tradeable in the first place.
rationales.B: The first trade, opened on 2 October 2014 when the spread crossed the -2 standard deviation mark, was closed on 18 November 2014 when the spread reached the moving average, and was profitable after slightly more than a month. The second trade was also profitable but lasted much longer. After the third trade was entered on 21 July 2015, however, there was a structural break: CP's decline further intensified while CNR stayed relatively flat, so the spread continued to narrow instead of reverting. The loss on that third trade could have been significantly greater than the combined profits from the first two transactions had the positions been closed before the spread finally mean-reverted in the spring of 2016. That asymmetry is the risk inherent in mean-reversion strategies, and it is why stop-loss discipline matters: the gains come in small, bounded increments when the spread behaves, while a single divergence that turns out to be structural rather than temporary can run far enough to swamp them.
rationales.C: Results were mixed rather than uniformly profitable, so the record does not validate the strategy unconditionally. Two of the three trades made money, but the third, entered on 21 July 2015, ran into a structural break in which CP's decline intensified while CNR stayed relatively flat and the spread kept narrowing; the loss on it could have exceeded the profits on the first two had the positions been closed before the spring 2016 reversion. Mean reversion is a bet on the divergence being temporary, not a certainty, and a structural change in one of the two businesses defeats it.

questions.stem: Market microstructure-based arbitrage strategies in the United States are most likely to:

options.A: hold positions for several months at a time.
options.B: lack a usable trade and quote data source.
options.C: mine the limit order book for very short-term mispricing.

rationales.A: The horizon is milliseconds, not months. A temporary imbalance between buy and sell orders may trigger a spike in share price that lasts for only a few milliseconds, and the mispricing disappears with the imbalance that created it, so a position held for months captures nothing of it and simply takes on directional risk instead. Multi-month holding periods belong to fundamental and factor-based strategies, whose signals come from valuation and company analysis rather than from the order book.
rationales.B: A suitable data source exists and is standard. In the United States many market microstructure-based arbitrage strategies are built on the NYSE Trade and Quote (TAQ) database, which records trades and quotes at the granularity these strategies need, and they often involve extensive analysis of the limit order book constructed from it. The constraint on this style of investing is not data availability but the analytical tools and high-frequency trading capability required to act on the signal before it decays.
rationales.C: These strategies take advantage of the NYSE Trade and Quote (TAQ) database and often involve extensive analysis of the limit order book to identify very short-term mispricing opportunities. For example, a temporary imbalance between buy and sell orders may trigger a spike in share price that lasts for only a few milliseconds. Only those investors with the analytical tools and trading capabilities for high-frequency trading are in a position to capture such opportunities, and they are captured usually within a portfolio of many stocks designed to take advantage of very short-term discrepancies, since any single discrepancy is far too small to matter on its own.

questions.stem: Event-driven strategies are most likely:

options.A: a subset of factor-based strategies.
options.B: purely discretionary, not rules-based, strategies.
options.C: strategies that fit none of the standard active categories.

rationales.A: Event-driven strategies, together with statistical arbitrage, are presented precisely as a category that does not fit neatly into the fundamental, quantitative, and factor-based categorizations. A factor-based strategy harvests a persistent, rewarded exposure such as value, momentum, size, or quality across a broad cross-section of stocks. Corporate events such as mergers and acquisitions, spin-offs, and restructurings are not rewarded factors of that sort: they are discrete, dated situations exploited opportunistically, one deal at a time, and the return comes from the resolution of the specific event rather than from a risk premium earned by holding an exposure.
rationales.B: These strategies rely on extensive use of quantitative data and are usually implemented in a systematic, rules-based way, although the fund manager's judgment can also be incorporated in making investment decisions. So the strategy is not purely discretionary; the usual case is a rules-based process with judgment layered on top, for example in sizing the position taken in an announced deal or in assessing the probability that it closes.
rationales.C: Event-driven strategies are a category of active strategies that do not fit neatly into the fundamental, quantitative, and factor-based categorizations. Along with statistical arbitrage, they rely on extensive use of quantitative data and are usually implemented in a systematic, rules-based way, but they can also incorporate the fund manager's judgment in making investment decisions. What sets them apart is the source of the opportunity: they exploit corporate events such as mergers and acquisitions, spin-offs, and restructurings, so the return depends on how a specific, dated situation resolves rather than on a valuation gap or a rewarded factor exposure.

questions.stem: Identifying pairs of stocks for pairs trading is most likely:

options.A: straightforward, because any two highly correlated stocks qualify.
options.B: the most difficult step, and done quantitatively or fundamentally.
options.C: possible only through fundamental analysis.

rationales.A: High historical correlation on its own can be coincidental, so it is not sufficient. A food retailer and a car manufacturer may show closely correlated prices with no business reason for the relationship to hold, and a comovement that rests on coincidence gives no reason for the spread to revert once it widens. A usable pair needs both statistical evidence of mean reversion and a fundamental reason for the two prices to move together, such as two food producers with comparable business prospects. The relationship also has to be intact: a bank that has brought in new management and been active in mergers and acquisitions has undergone a fundamental change that invalidates its historical relationship with a former partner, however strong the past correlation looks. Identification is in fact the most difficult aspect of the strategy, not a straightforward one.
rationales.B: Identification of the pairs is the most difficult aspect of a pairs-trading strategy. It can be done either by using a quantitative approach and creating models of stock prices, testing the ratio or log spread for mean reversion, or by using a fundamental approach to judge the two stocks whose prices should move together for qualitative reasons. The best candidates satisfy both tests. Two food producers with comparable business prospects and a price ratio that has reverted to its mean in the past qualify on the statistical and the fundamental criterion alike. A food retailer paired with a car manufacturer fails the fundamental test, because a cross-industry correlation of that kind is likely coincidental. A bank that has recently changed management and engaged in merger activity fails too, because the fundamental change breaks the historical relationship the trade would be relying on.
rationales.C: Fundamental judgment is one of two routes, not the only one. Pairs can equally be identified by a quantitative approach, creating models of stock prices and testing the spread or price ratio for mean reversion, and in practice a quantitative screen is often the starting point, with fundamental analysis then confirming that there is an economic reason for the two prices to move together and that no structural change has broken the relationship. Ruling out statistical models would discard half the available toolkit.

questions.stem: The primary risk in pairs trading is most likely:

options.A: rapid mean reversion of the spread.
options.B: a divergence that is not temporary.
options.C: a decline in both legs in a market selloff.

rationales.A: Rapid mean reversion is the outcome the trade is designed to capture, not a risk. The position is closed when the spread returns to its moving average, so the sooner that happens the sooner the profit is realized and the capital is released for the next opportunity. The danger runs in the opposite direction, toward divergence that persists for structural reasons, which is why stop-loss rules are used to cap the loss rather than reversion-speed limits.
rationales.B: The biggest risk in pairs trading, and in most other mean-reversion strategies, is that the observed price divergence is not temporary but is instead due to structural reasons. For example, the outperformance of one stock might be due to the fact that the company has developed a new technology or product that cannot be easily replicated by competitors; in that case the spread is not a dislocation waiting to close but a permanent repricing, and the short leg keeps losing as the long leg stands still. Because risk management is critical for the success of such strategies, investors often employ stop-loss rules to exit trades when a loss limit is reached, which bounds the damage from a divergence that turns out to be structural while leaving the profitable reversions to run to the moving average.
rationales.C: A pairs trade is long one stock and short the other in comparable size, so a broad market selloff largely nets out across the two legs: the strategy is close to market neutral by construction, which is what allows it to be judged on the spread alone rather than on market direction. The exposure that matters is to the relationship between the two stocks, and the biggest risk is that an observed divergence in that relationship is structural rather than temporary.

drills.los_text: describe how fundamental active investment strategies are created

questions.stem: Steps in creating a fundamental active investment strategy most likely start with:

options.A: constructing a portfolio and applying buy and sell disciplines.
options.B: defining the universe and building research infrastructure.
options.C: forecasting cash flows and estimating intrinsic values.

rationales.A: Constructing a portfolio with the desired risk profile, and applying the buy and sell disciplines that maintain it, are the final steps of the process, together with ongoing monitoring and rebalancing. Putting them first reverses the actual sequence, which begins by defining the investment universe, prescreening it to a workable list, and building a research infrastructure capable of analyzing what survives the screen. There is no risk profile to construct toward until the candidate securities exist and have been valued.
rationales.B: The process begins with defining the investment universe, prescreening that universe, and building an appropriate research infrastructure; only then do forecasting, valuation, portfolio construction, and the buy and sell disciplines follow. A growth-oriented prescreen illustrates what the second step does in practice, with criteria such as the following: the year-over-year growth rate in earnings per share from continuing operations has increased over each of the last four fiscal years; growth in earnings per share from continuing operations over the last 12 months has been positive; the percentage difference between the actual announced earnings and the consensus earnings estimate for the most recent quarter is greater than or equal to 10%; the percentage change in stock price over the last four weeks is positive; the 26-week relative price strength is greater than or equal to the industry's 26-week relative price strength; and the average daily volume for the last 10 days is in the top 50% of the market. Screens of that kind cut a broad universe down to the names the research infrastructure can realistically cover in depth.
rationales.C: Forecasting company cash flows and converting those forecasts into intrinsic value estimates are later steps. They come after the universe has been defined, prescreened down to a manageable set of candidates, and a research infrastructure has been built to support the forecasts, because there is nothing to forecast until the candidate list exists and no reliable way to forecast it until the data, models, and analyst coverage are in place.

questions.stem: A manager prescreens his universe for accelerating year-over-year growth in earnings per share, positive earnings surprises, positive recent price strength, and at least average liquidity, with no valuation screen. The mandate is most likely:

options.A: value oriented.
options.B: style neutral.
options.C: growth oriented.

rationales.A: Nothing in the screen is value oriented. A value investor's screening criteria would typically include a rule to screen out issues that are expensively valued relative to earnings or assets, and the absence of any valuation multiple here is telling. The price criteria point the other way as well: screening for a positive percentage change in stock price over the last four weeks, and for 26-week relative price strength at least equal to the industry's, selects names that have already run rather than names trading at depressed prices.
rationales.B: The screen expresses a clear style. Every criterion selects either for earnings growth or for the persistence of that growth in reported results and in the share price, which is a growth orientation, and the one criterion that is not about growth, average daily volume in the top 50% of the market, is a liquidity filter rather than a style choice. A style-neutral mandate would not stack four growth and momentum criteria in a row, nor would it leave valuation entirely unscreened.
rationales.C: The manager has a growth orientation, with a focus on companies that have delivered earnings per share growth in recent years and that have maintained their earnings and price growth momentum. The first criterion specifies accelerating earnings per share growth rates over recent fiscal years, requiring that the year-over-year growth rate from continuing operations increased over each of the last four fiscal years, while the second discards companies for which recent earnings growth has been negative over the last 12 months. The third screens for companies that have beaten consensus earnings expectations, a percentage difference between actual announced earnings and the consensus estimate of at least 10% in the most recent quarter; a positive earnings surprise suggests that past earnings growth is continuing. The fourth and fifth criteria screen for positive recent stock price momentum, a positive four-week price change and 26-week relative price strength at or above the industry's. The sixth, average daily volume for the last 10 days in the top 50% of the market, retains only stocks with at least average market liquidity. Note the absence of any valuation multiples among the screening criteria: a value investor's screening criteria would typically include a rule to screen out issues that are expensively valued relative to earnings or assets.

questions.stem: Confirmation bias, also referred to as stock love bias, is most likely:

options.A: a cognitive error of seeking confirming information.
options.B: an emotional bias rooted in fear of loss.
options.C: not a documented behavioral bias.

rationales.A: Confirmation bias is a cognitive error: the tendency of analysts and investors to look for information that confirms their existing beliefs about their favorite companies and to ignore or undervalue any information that contradicts those beliefs. The behavior creates selective exposure, selective perception, and selective retention, and may be thought of as a selection bias, since the evidence the investor ends up reasoning from is not a fair sample of the evidence available. Some of the consequences are a poorly diversified portfolio, excessive risk exposure, and continued holdings in poorly performing securities, because contrary news about a favored name is discounted rather than acted on. Actively seeking out the opinions of other investors or team members, and looking for information from a range of sources to challenge existing beliefs, may reduce the risk of confirmation bias.
rationales.B: It is a cognitive error rather than an emotional bias: the failure is in how information is gathered and processed, not in an emotional reaction to the prospect of loss. The investor reasons from a biased sample of evidence, having sought out what confirms the existing view of a favored company and discounted what contradicts it. Because the error is informational, the remedies are informational too, such as deliberately seeking contrary opinions and widening the range of sources, whereas emotional biases are usually addressed by rules and constraints on behavior.
rationales.C: Confirmation bias is among the better documented biases in behavioral finance and is named in the equity management literature as stock love bias. It describes a specific and observable pattern: seeking out evidence that supports existing beliefs about favorite companies while ignoring or undervaluing evidence that contradicts them, producing selective exposure, perception, and retention, with poor diversification and persistent holdings in underperforming securities as consequences.

questions.stem: The illusion of control bias is most likely:

options.A: a bias with no accepted definition.
options.B: a cognitive error of overestimating personal success odds.
options.C: not a recognized behavioral bias.

rationales.A: The bias has an accepted and widely quoted definition. Langer (1983) defines the illusion of control bias as an expectancy of a personal success probability inappropriately higher than the objective probability would warrant, and the literature on active equity management uses that formulation directly: the bias is the human tendency to overestimate one's ability to control or influence outcomes. The definition is also specific enough to be operational, since it identifies the error as a gap between the subjective success probability and the objective one.
rationales.B: The illusion of control is a cognitive error, defined by Langer (1983) as an expectancy of a personal success probability inappropriately higher than the objective probability would warrant. The basic philosophy behind active equity management is that investors believe they can control or at least influence outcomes, and skilled investors have a healthy confidence in their own ability to select stocks and expect to outperform the market; the illusion of control bias refers to the human tendency to overestimate those abilities. Having an illusion of control could lead to excessive trading, because each decision is believed to add value, and to heavy weighting on a few stocks, because conviction is mistaken for edge. Investors should seek contrary viewpoints and set and enforce proper trading and portfolio diversification rules to try to avoid this problem.
rationales.C: It is a recognized and named bias. Langer (1983) identified and defined it, and it is treated in the active equity management literature as a cognitive error with specific portfolio consequences, chiefly excessive trading and heavy concentration in a few stocks, along with specific remedies, namely seeking contrary viewpoints and enforcing trading and diversification rules.

questions.stem: Loss aversion is most likely:

options.A: a bias that prompts early sale of losing positions.
options.B: an emotional bias favoring loss avoidance over gains.
options.C: a cognitive error.

rationales.A: Loss aversion produces the opposite behavior. Poorly performing positions are maintained in the hope of potential recovery, while successful investments are sold and the gains realized prematurely in order to avoid further risk. Deliberately realizing losses early is a tax-management decision, not a description of this bias.
rationales.B: Loss aversion is an emotional bias whereby investors tend to prefer avoiding losses over achieving gains. A number of studies on loss aversion suggest that, psychologically, losses are significantly more powerful than gains: in absolute value terms, the utility derived from a gain is much lower than the utility given up in an equivalent loss. The bias can cause investors to hold unbalanced portfolios in which poorly performing positions are maintained in the hope of potential recovery and successful investments are sold, with the gains realized, prematurely in order to avoid further risk. A disciplined trading strategy with firmly established stop-loss rules is essential to prevent fundamental investors from falling into this trap.
rationales.C: Loss aversion sits in the emotional bias category rather than among the cognitive errors. It arises from the asymmetric psychological weight of losses and gains, not from faulty information processing or reasoning, which is why it is addressed with stop-loss discipline rather than with better information.

questions.stem: Overconfidence bias is most likely:

options.A: not a recognized investor bias.
options.B: an emotional bias of unwarranted faith in one's own judgment.
options.C: the illusion of control under another name.

rationales.A: Overconfidence is one of the recognized emotional biases. It means that the portfolio manager underestimates risks and overestimates expected returns, and it is commonly associated with overtrading.
rationales.B: Overconfidence bias is an emotional bias whereby investors demonstrate unwarranted faith in their own intuitive reasoning, judgment, and/or cognitive abilities. This overconfidence may be the result of overestimating knowledge levels, abilities, and access to information. Unlike the illusion of control bias, which is a cognitive error, overconfidence bias is an illusion of exaggerated knowledge and abilities. Investors may, for example, attribute success to their own ability rather than to luck. Such bias means that the portfolio manager underestimates risks and overestimates expected returns. Regularly reviewing actual investment records and seeking constructive feedback from other professionals can help investors gain awareness of this self-attribution tendency.
rationales.C: The two are related but distinct. Overconfidence bias is an emotional bias and an illusion of exaggerated knowledge and ability across one's reasoning and judgment generally; illusion of control bias is a cognitive error and concerns the belief that one can influence outcomes. They are not two labels for the same bias.

questions.stem: Availability bias is most likely:

options.A: an information-processing bias that substitutes ease of recall for probability.
options.B: an emotional bias driven by attachment to familiar companies.
options.C: not a recognized behavioral phenomenon.

rationales.A: Availability bias is an information-processing bias whereby individuals take a mental shortcut in estimating the probability of an outcome based on the availability of the information and how easily the outcome comes to mind. Easily recalled outcomes are often perceived as being more likely than those that are harder to recall or understand, and the bias falls in the cognitive error category. In fundamental equity investing, it may reduce the investment opportunity set and result in insufficient diversification, as the portfolio manager relies on familiar stocks that reflect a narrow range of experience. Setting an appropriate investment strategy in line with the investment horizon, as well as conducting a disciplined portfolio analysis with a long-term focus, will help eliminate any short-term over-emphasis caused by this bias.
rationales.B: Availability bias is an information-processing shortcut and therefore a cognitive error, not an emotional bias: ease of recall stands in for probability. The familiarity it produces, reliance on well-known stocks reflecting a narrow range of experience, is a consequence of that faulty processing rather than of emotional attachment.
rationales.C: Availability bias is a standard element of the behavioral taxonomy, classified among the cognitive errors: the probability of an outcome is judged by how readily examples of it come to mind.

questions.stem: Regret aversion bias is most likely:

options.A: an emotional bias that deters decisions feared to turn out poorly.
options.B: a bias that drives excessive trading in pursuit of every opportunity.
options.C: a cognitive error.

rationales.A: Regret aversion bias is an emotional bias that causes investors to avoid making decisions they fear will turn out poorly; put simply, investors try to avoid the pain of regret associated with bad decisions. The bias may actually prevent investors from making decisions at all. They may instead hold on to positions for too long and, in the meantime, lose out on profitable investment opportunities. A carefully defined portfolio review process can help mitigate its effects. Such a process might, for example, require investors to periodically review and justify existing positions or to substantiate the decision not to have exposure to other stocks in the universe.
rationales.B: Regret aversion tends to prevent decisions rather than multiply them. Investors hold on to positions for too long and lose out on profitable investment opportunities; trading excessively in pursuit of every opportunity is not the behavior this bias produces.
rationales.C: Regret aversion is classified as an emotional bias, not a cognitive error. It is driven by the anticipated pain of regret rather than by faulty reasoning or information processing, which is why a disciplined review process, rather than better information, is what mitigates it.

drills.los_text: describe how quantitative active investment strategies are created

questions.stem: The history of quantitative active equity investing is most likely:

options.A: a setback in the March 2000 dot-com collapse known as the quant meltdown.
options.B: an origin in the 2008 global financial crisis.
options.C: an origin in the 1970s and mainstream adoption thereafter.

rationales.A: The quant meltdown refers to the significant losses many quantitative equity funds suffered in August 2007, not to the March 2000 dot-com collapse.
rationales.B: Quantitative active equity investing began in the 1970s and was a mainstream approach for decades before the global financial crisis. The crisis contributed to growing suspicions about the sustainability of quantitative investing rather than launching the approach.
rationales.C: Quantitative active equity investing began in the 1970s and became a mainstream investment approach in the subsequent decades. Many quantitative equity funds suffered significant losses in August 2007, an event that became known as the quant meltdown, and the subsequent global financial crisis contributed to growing suspicions about the sustainability of quantitative investing. Both the performance and the perception of the approach have recovered significantly since 2012, as managers improved their research, processes, and portfolio construction and began to use unconventional data sources more effectively.

questions.stem: The data commonly used in quantitative investing most likely fall into:

options.A: company mapping, fundamentals, survey data, and unconventional data.
options.B: historical prices alone.
options.C: no distinguishable categories.

rationales.A: The most commonly used data in quantitative investing typically fall into four categories. Company mapping is used to track many companies over time and across data vendors: each company may have multiple classes of shares, new companies go public while some existing ones disappear through bankruptcies, mergers, or takeovers, company names, ticker symbols, and other identifiers can change over time, and different data vendors have their own unique identifiers. Company fundamentals include company demographics, financial statements, and other market data such as price, dividends, stock splits, and trading volume; quantitative managers almost never collect these themselves and instead rely on vendors such as Capital IQ, Compustat, Worldscope, Reuters, FactSet, and Bloomberg. Survey data include details of corporate earnings, forecasts and estimates by various market participants, macroeconomic variables, sentiment indicators, and information on funds flow. Unconventional, or unstructured, data include satellite images, measures of news sentiment, customer-supplier chain metrics, and corporate events, among many other types of information.
rationales.B: Prices are one input only, and they sit within company fundamentals alongside dividends, stock splits, and trading volume. Company mapping across vendors and share classes, survey and estimate data, and unconventional or unstructured data are distinct categories in their own right.
rationales.C: The data are grouped into identifiable categories: company mapping, company fundamentals, survey data, and unconventional or unstructured data.

questions.stem: Regarding the Pearson IC and the Spearman rank IC, the most likely statement is that:

options.A: the two are not distinguished from each other.
options.B: the Pearson IC correlates factor scores with next period's returns.
options.C: the two are identical measures computed on the same inputs.

rationales.A: The two measures are distinguished explicitly, including their different sensitivity to extreme values: the Pearson IC is sensitive to outliers, while the Spearman rank IC is a similar but more robust measure and is often preferred by practitioners.
rationales.B: The Pearson IC is the simple correlation coefficient between the factor scores, essentially standardized exposures, for the current period and the next period's stock returns. Because it is a correlation coefficient, its value always lies between -1 and +1, or, expressed in percentage terms, between -100% and +100%. The higher the IC, the higher the predictive power of the factor for subsequent returns; as a simple rule of thumb, in relation to US equities any factor with an average monthly IC of 5%-6% is considered very strong. The coefficient is sensitive to outliers. A similar but more robust measure is the Spearman rank IC, which is essentially the Pearson correlation coefficient between the ranked factor scores and the ranked forward returns.
rationales.C: They are computed on different inputs. The Pearson IC correlates the factor scores themselves with subsequent returns and is therefore sensitive to outliers; the Spearman rank IC correlates the ranked factor scores with the ranked forward returns and is more robust, which is why practitioners often prefer it.

questions.stem: In one month, a sample of stocks ranked by earnings yield is generally in line with subsequent returns for every stock but one, whose highest factor score is paired with the worst return. For that month, the Pearson IC and the Spearman rank IC are most likely:

options.A: unaffected by the outlier.
options.B: identical to each other.
options.C: opposite in sign, with the Pearson IC negative.

rationales.A: A single extreme observation is exactly what moves these two measures apart. The Pearson IC is sensitive to outliers, so the stock for which the factor predicts the highest return but which turns out to be the worst performer drags that coefficient down; the rank IC, computed on ranks, is far less affected. Neither coefficient is left unaffected in the same way.
rationales.B: The two diverge. The single outlier drags the Pearson IC to -0.8%, which suggests that the signal did not perform well and was negatively correlated with the subsequent month's returns, while the Spearman rank IC for the same sample is 40%, suggesting strong predictive power. A measure computed on scores and a measure computed on ranks do not take the same value when an outlier is present.
rationales.C: The Pearson IC is negative at -0.8%, suggesting on its own that the signal did not perform well and was negatively correlated with the subsequent month's returns. Looking more carefully, however, the factor is generally in line with subsequent stock returns, with the exception of the one stock for which the factor predicts the highest return but which turns out to be the worst performer. A single outlier can therefore turn what may actually be a good factor into a bad one, because the Pearson IC is sensitive to outliers. The Spearman rank IC, by contrast, is 40%, suggesting that the factor has strong predictive power for subsequent returns. If three equally weighted portfolios had been constructed, the long basket of the three highest-scoring stocks would have outperformed the short basket of the three lowest-scoring stocks by 56 bps in this period, a long/short tercile return of 0.56%.

questions.stem: For factor selection and weighting in a multifactor model, Qian, Hua, and Sorensen (2007) most likely propose:

options.A: treating each factor as an asset.
options.B: using a single factor.
options.C: weighting all factors equally.

rationales.A: Qian, Hua, and Sorensen (2007) propose treating each factor as an asset; factor weighting therefore becomes an asset allocation decision. A standard mean-variance optimization can also be used to weight factors. Deciding which factors to include and how to weight them is a critical piece of the strategy, and investors should bear in mind that factors may be effective individually yet add no material value to a factor model because they are correlated with other factors.
rationales.B: Their proposal concerns the construction of a multifactor model: each factor is treated as an asset, so that weighting the factors becomes an asset allocation decision. Studying the efficacy of single factors is the step that precedes the choice of which factors to include, not the proposal itself.
rationales.C: Equal weighting is neither their proposal nor forced on the manager. They propose treating each factor as an asset, making factor weighting an asset allocation decision, and a standard mean-variance optimization can also be used to weight factors. Factors can be selected and weighted using either qualitative or systematic processes.

questions.stem: The portfolio construction issues in quantitative investment most likely include:

options.A: trading costs but not risk models.
options.B: risk models and trading costs.
options.C: no issues beyond building the alpha model.

rationales.A: Estimating the variance-covariance structure of stock returns is central to quantitative portfolio construction rather than dispensable. Directly estimating that matrix from sample return data typically is infeasible and suffers from significant estimation errors, which is why managers rely on commercial factor risk models; diversification does not substitute for the estimate.
rationales.B: Risk models estimate the variance-covariance matrix of stock returns, that is, the risk of every stock and the correlation among stocks. Directly estimating that matrix using sample return data typically is infeasible and suffers from significant estimation errors, so managers generally rely on commercial risk model vendors for these data; MSCI Barra and Axioma are examples of such data providers. Trading costs are the second issue. There are two kinds: explicit costs, such as commissions, fees, and taxes, and implicit costs, such as the bid-ask spread and market impact. When two stocks have similar expected returns and risks, normally the one with lower execution costs is preferred.
rationales.C: Risk model estimation and transaction cost modeling are both named portfolio construction issues, and they remain to be addressed after the alpha model has been built.

questions.stem: Survivorship bias, look-ahead bias, data mining, and overfitting are most likely:

options.A: issues relevant only to fundamental analysis.
options.B: common pitfalls in quantitative investment processes.
options.C: issues posing no risk to quantitative back-tests.

rationales.A: All four are pitfalls of quantitative research design specifically. Each one arises from the way a back-test is built out of a historical database, which is the core of a quantitative process rather than of fundamental research. Survivorship bias comes from the construction of the test universe, look-ahead bias from the timing of the data fed into the test, and data mining and overfitting from the search over that data for a pattern. A fundamental analyst can be fooled by the same effects, but they are defined and documented as failures of quantitative decision making.
rationales.B: These are the common pitfalls in quantitative investment processes. Survivorship bias is one of the most common issues affecting quantitative decision making: when back-tests use only those companies that are currently in business today, they ignore the stocks that have left the investment universe through bankruptcy, delisting, or acquisition, so only the companies that survived are tested and the strategy is assumed never to have invested in companies that failed. That bias often leads to overly optimistic results and sometimes causes investors to draw outright wrong conclusions. The second major issue in back-testing is look-ahead bias, which results from using information that was unknown or unavailable at the time an investment decision was made - for example, using a company's financial accounting data at a point in time before the data were actually released. In computer science, data mining refers to automated computational processes for discovering patterns in large datasets, often involving sophisticated statistical techniques, computation algorithms, and large-scale database systems. In finance, the same excessive search of past financial data to uncover patterns that conform to a pre-determined model introduces a bias that results in model overfitting, a model fitted to noise that does not survive out of sample.
rationales.C: Each of the four is a documented risk to back-tests, which is precisely why they are the canonical quantitative pitfalls: testing only today's survivors, using information that was not yet available at the decision date, and extracting patterns that fit noise rather than signal. The back-test is where the damage is done, because the historical sample is the only evidence a quantitative process has before capital is committed, and an optimistic back-test is what persuades an investor to fund the strategy.

questions.stem: A long/short strategy that buys the Japanese dividend payers with the worst returns in the previous month and shorts those with the highest returns is most likely to:

options.A: be largely unaffected by transaction costs.
options.B: beat a price-to-book strategy before transaction costs.
options.C: lose no more return to costs than a price-to-book strategy.

rationales.A: Trading is not free, and transaction costs can easily erode returns significantly. Short-term reversal - stocks that have performed well recently, say in the last month, are more likely to revert and underperform in the subsequent month - has been found to be a good stock selection signal in the Japanese equity market before transaction costs, but the signal is defined over one month and so requires rebuilding both legs every month. In a theoretical world with no transaction costs the long/short version generated an annual return of 12%; changing the transaction cost assumption from 0 bps to 30 bps per trade makes that return drop sharply. The long and short legs do not offset each other's costs: each leg pays to get in and to get out, so a two-sided portfolio incurs roughly double the trading, not none of it.
rationales.B: In a theoretical world with no transaction costs, this simple long/short strategy - buying the top 20% of dividend-paying stocks in Japan with the worst performance in the previous month and shorting the bottom 20% with the highest returns in the previous month - generated an annual return of 12%, beating the classic value factor of price to book. That gross result is what makes short-term reversal look like an attractive selection signal in this market. The picture changes once costs are charged: if the transaction cost assumption is changed from 0 bps to 30 bps per trade, the return of the reversal strategy drops sharply while the return of the price-to-book strategy drops only modestly, because a monthly reversal signal demands high turnover of both legs and a price-to-book signal is slow moving.
rationales.C: Reversal loses far more to costs than price to book does. At a cost assumption of 0 bps per trade the reversal strategy's 12% annual return beats the price-to-book factor; at 30 bps per trade the reversal return drops sharply while the price-to-book return drops only modestly, and the ranking reverses. The difference is turnover. A signal built from the previous month's returns reshuffles both the long and the short leg every month, so the 30 bps is paid over and over, whereas price to book changes slowly and leaves the portfolio largely in place.

questions.stem: Equity styles are most likely defined by:

options.A: pairs of common attributes, such as value and growth.
options.B: no identifiable attribute.
options.C: a single attribute, the price-to-earnings multiple.

rationales.A: Equity styles are defined by pairs of common attributes, such as value and growth, large cap and small cap, high volatility and low volatility, high dividend and low dividend, or developed markets and emerging markets. Style pairs need not be mutually exclusive, so a stock can sit on the value side of one pair and the small-cap side of another at the same time. Each pair interprets stock performance from a different perspective, and a combination of several style pairs may often give a more complete picture of the sources of stock returns than any single pair can.
rationales.B: Styles are defined, and the attribute pairs that define them organize most of style analysis: value and growth, large cap and small cap, high volatility and low volatility, high dividend and low dividend, developed markets and emerging markets. Holdings-based and returns-based style analysis, the style boxes, and the commercial style indexes are all built on those attributes, with providers scoring stocks on them and assigning style classifications or inclusion factors accordingly.
rationales.C: Styles come in attribute pairs rather than from one multiple. Price to earnings is only one of several valuation inputs used on the value side - price to book, price to sales, price to cash flow, and dividend yield sit alongside it - and the pairs extend well beyond valuation to size, volatility, dividend level, and market development. A single multiple cannot express the large cap versus small cap or developed versus emerging market dimensions at all, and it cannot capture a stock that carries characteristics of two styles at once.

questions.stem: Style analysis is most likely conducted using:

options.A: the returns-based approach only.
options.B: no analytical approach, only index providers' classifications.
options.C: both the holdings-based and returns-based approaches.

rationales.A: Two approaches are in general use, not one, and each has its own strengths and weaknesses. Portfolio holdings are not universally proprietary: current constituents are frequently available, and point-in-time databases carry historical constituents and historical style definitions, which is what makes holdings-based analysis workable and indeed the more accurate of the two. The returns-based approach is the one that can be applied when portfolio holdings are not disclosed, which is a reason both approaches exist side by side rather than a reason to drop one of them.
rationales.B: Both a holdings-based and a returns-based approach are available to the analyst. The holdings-based approach aggregates the attributes of the individual stocks in the portfolio bottom-up and is generally more accurate, but it requires the availability of all the portfolio constituents as well as the style attributes of each stock. The returns-based approach compares the returns of the strategy with a set of style indexes and can be applied when portfolio holdings are not disclosed. Index providers' classifications are inputs to this work - the style indexes a returns-based regression runs against, and the stock-level style attributes a holdings-based aggregation uses - not a substitute for it.
rationales.C: The two main approaches used in style analysis are the holdings-based approach and the returns-based approach, and each has its own strengths and weaknesses. An equity investment style is the aggregation of attributes from the individual stocks in the portfolio, so holdings-based analysis is done bottom-up; it is more accurate, but it requires the availability of all the portfolio constituents and the style attributes of each stock. The returns-based approach compares the returns of the strategy with a set of style indexes and can be applied when portfolio holdings are not disclosed. The holdings-based approach is executed differently by the various commercial information providers, and using different criteria or different sources for the underlying value and growth numbers may lead to slightly different classifications for the same stock. Morningstar and Thomson Reuters Lipper define the style of an individual stock with a 0/1 attribute: a stock's attribute for a specific style is 1 if it is included in that style index and 0 otherwise. MSCI and FTSE Russell instead assume a stock can have the characteristics of two styles, such as value and growth, at the same time, using a multifactor approach to assign style inclusion factors to each stock.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the Morningstar Style Box is most likely correct?

options.A: It splits the stock universe along market capitalization only.
options.B: It relies on returns-based style analysis.
options.C: It helps investors and advisers identify a fund's investment style.

rationales.A: The Style Box splits the stock universe along both style dimensions at once, not one. One pair divides the universe into value, core (or blend for funds), and growth; the same universe can be split by another style definition, large cap, mid cap, and small cap. Crossing the two creates a grid of nine squares - three investment styles for each of three size categories - rather than a single three-square column, so size accounts for only one axis of the classification.
rationales.B: The Style Box uses holdings-based style analysis. Morningstar determines a stock's value and growth scores from five stock attributes each, working from the securities actually held, and classifies about the same number of stocks into each of the value, core, and growth styles. A returns-based approach would instead regress the fund's return series against a set of style indexes and never look at a holding, which is not how the Style Box is built.
rationales.C: The Morningstar Style Box first appeared in 1992 to help investors and advisers determine the investment style of a fund. In a style box, each style pair splits the stock universe into two or three groups, such as value, core (or blend), and growth, and the same universe can be split by another style definition, such as large cap, mid cap, and small cap. The Morningstar Style Box splits the universe along both dimensions, creating a grid of nine squares: a nine-square grid featuring three stock investment styles for each of three size categories, large, mid, and small. Two of the three style categories, value and growth, are common to both stocks and funds, while the central column is labeled core for stocks - those for which neither value nor growth characteristics dominate - and blend for funds. It uses holdings-based style analysis, classifies about the same number of stocks in each of the value, core, and growth styles, and determines the value and growth scores by using five stock attributes.

questions.stem: The boundaries between large-, mid-, and small-cap stocks are most likely:

options.A: set so each group holds about a third of universe capitalization.
options.B: set by regulation at a uniform global threshold.
options.C: set differently by different data and research providers.

rationales.A: Common practice is nowhere near equal thirds. One practice is to define large-cap stocks as those that account for the top ~70% of the capitalization of all stocks in the universe, with mid-cap stocks representing the next ~20% and small-cap stocks accounting for the balance, roughly the last ~10%. Splitting capitalization into equal thirds would push far larger and more mature companies into the small-cap bucket than any provider does, and it would misdescribe the economics the categories are meant to capture.
rationales.B: No regulatory or universal threshold exists. Size classification is determined by the company's market capitalization, but there is no consensus on what the size thresholds for the different categories should be, and different data and research providers use different criteria for size classification purposes. A single stated currency cutoff applied globally would also break down across markets, because the capitalization distribution of the local universe differs from one market to another, which is why the common conventions are expressed as shares of universe capitalization instead.
rationales.C: There is no consensus on the boundaries that separate large-, mid-, and small-cap companies. The size classification is determined by the company's market capitalization, but there is no agreement on what the thresholds should be, and different data and research providers use different criteria for size classification purposes. One practice is to define large-cap stocks as those that account for the top ~70% of the capitalization of all stocks in the universe, with mid-cap stocks representing the next ~20% and small-cap stocks accounting for the balance. The categories differ in economics as well as in threshold: large-cap companies tend to be well established, with a strong market presence, good information disclosure, and extensive analyst and media scrutiny, which brings lower risk but more limited future growth potential, while small-cap companies tend to be less mature, with potentially greater growth, a higher risk of failure, and lower analyst and public scrutiny.

questions.stem: Morningstar's value score for a stock is most likely based on:

options.A: components that Morningstar does not disclose.
options.B: forward-looking and historical measures in equal weight.
options.C: trailing price-to-earnings alone.

rationales.A: The scoring scheme is published component by component. The value score is half forward-looking and half historical: price to projected earnings carries the whole 50.0% forward-looking half, and price to book, price to sales, price to cash flow, and dividend yield carry 12.5% each in the historical half. The growth score is built the same way, with long-term projected earnings growth at 50.0% forward-looking and historical earnings growth, sales growth, cash flow growth, and book value growth at 12.5% each. Both scores are then scaled to a range of 0 to 100 and differenced to give the net style score.
rationales.B: The value score is 50% forward-looking and 50% historical. The forward-looking half is price to projected earnings at 50.0%; the historical half is price to book 12.5%, price to sales 12.5%, price to cash flow 12.5%, and dividend yield 12.5%. The growth score mirrors that structure: forward-looking measures 50.0%, consisting of long-term projected earnings growth at 50.0%, and historical measures 50.0%, consisting of historical earnings growth 12.5%, sales growth 12.5%, cash flow growth 12.5%, and book value growth 12.5%. The scores are scaled to a range of 0 to 100, and the difference between the stock's growth and value scores is called the net style score. If the net style score is strongly negative, approaching -100, the stock is classified as value; if it is strongly positive, the stock is classified as growth; if the value and growth scores are similar in strength, the net style score is close to zero and the stock is classified as core.
rationales.C: Trailing price to earnings is not even one of the inputs. The forward-looking half of the value score is price to projected earnings, weighted 50.0%, and the historical half spreads 12.5% each across price to book, price to sales, price to cash flow, and dividend yield. One multiple could not produce the 0-to-100 scaling of value and growth scores, nor the net style score difference that classifies a stock as value, core, or growth, and it would ignore the dividend and sales evidence the scheme deliberately includes.

questions.stem: The value style in the MSCI World Value and Growth Indexes is most likely defined using:

options.A: no specified variables.
options.B: book-value-to-price, forward earnings-to-price, and dividend yield.
options.C: dividend yield alone.

rationales.A: The variables are specified exactly, three for value and five for growth. The value investment style characteristics for index construction are defined using the book-value-to-price ratio, the 12-month forward-earnings-to-price ratio, and dividend yield. The growth style characteristics are defined using the long-term forward EPS growth rate, the short-term forward EPS growth rate, the current internal growth rate, the long-term historical EPS growth trend, and the long-term historical sales-per-share growth trend. Z-scores for each variable are calculated and aggregated for each security to determine that security's overall style characteristics.
rationales.B: The value investment style characteristics for index construction are defined using three variables: the book-value-to-price ratio, the 12-month forward-earnings-to-price ratio, and dividend yield. Growth is defined using five variables: the long-term forward EPS growth rate, the short-term forward EPS growth rate, the current internal growth rate, the long-term historical EPS growth trend, and the long-term historical sales-per-share growth trend. Z-scores for each variable are calculated and aggregated for each security to determine the security's overall style characteristics. A security need not fall wholly on one side: a stock assigned a value inclusion factor of 0.6 has both value and growth characteristics and contributes 60% to the performance of the value index and 40% to the growth index.
rationales.C: Dividend yield is one of the three value variables, alongside the book-value-to-price ratio and the 12-month forward-earnings-to-price ratio, and the three are combined as z-scores aggregated for each security. Yield alone would classify every high payer as value whatever its book or earnings multiple showed, and it would leave the five growth variables - long-term and short-term forward EPS growth, the current internal growth rate, and the long-term historical EPS and sales-per-share growth trends - with nothing on the value side to be weighed against when the value inclusion factor is set.

questions.stem: Compared with returns-based style analysis, holdings-based style analysis is most likely:

options.A: more accurate.
options.B: less accurate.
options.C: more widely applicable.

rationales.A: Holdings-based style analysis is generally more accurate than returns-based analysis because it uses the actual portfolio holdings: an equity investment style is the aggregation of attributes from the individual stocks in the portfolio, and the holdings-based approach measures those attributes bottom-up instead of inferring them from a return series. Morningstar studies have concluded that it generally produces more accurate results, although there may be exceptions. Kaplan (2011) argued that most returns-based style analysis models impose unnecessary constraints that limit the results within certain boundaries, making it difficult to detect more aggressive positions such as deep value or micro cap. The accuracy comes at a cost in data: holdings-based analysis requires the availability of all the portfolio constituents as well as the style attributes of each stock, and an analyst tracking historical changes in style needs point-in-time databases for both the constituents of the fund and the stocks' style definitions. The limited availability of data on derivatives also makes it less effective for funds with substantial positions in derivatives. Ideally, practitioners use both approaches: returns-based models can often be more widely applied, while holdings-based models allow deeper style analysis.
rationales.B: Holdings-based analysis is generally the more accurate of the two, because it works from the actual holdings rather than inferring exposures from a return series, and Morningstar studies have reached that conclusion. Derivatives are a genuine weakness of the holdings-based approach - the limited availability of data on derivatives often makes it less effective for funds with substantial derivative positions - but that is a specific exception for derivative-heavy funds rather than a general accuracy advantage for returns-based analysis, which still only compares the strategy's returns with a set of style indexes and can miss aggressive positions such as deep value or micro cap.
rationales.C: The two descriptions are swapped. Returns-based analysis is the approach that needs only the fund's return history, compared with a set of style indexes, which is why it can often be more widely applied, including to funds that do not disclose their holdings. Holdings-based analysis requires the availability of all the portfolio constituents as well as the style attributes of each stock, plus point-in-time databases if historical changes in style are to be tracked, so its reach is narrower even though it is more accurate and allows deeper style analysis where the data exist.

questions.stem: A manager's self-identification of investment style is most likely:

options.A: sufficient on its own.
options.B: disregarded by analysts.
options.C: drawn from the fund prospectus.

rationales.A: Self-identification is a starting point that gets checked. The fund's investment strategy is usually described in the fund prospectus and can be used to identify the fund's investment objective, which can be regarded as the manager's self-identification of the investment style; returns-based or holdings-based style analysis is then commonly used to identify the style actually being run, such as value/growth or large cap/small cap, and to determine whether it corresponds to the manager's self-identified style. That verification step is the reason the analysis is performed at all, so the stated style cannot stand on its own.
rationales.B: Self-identification is used rather than discarded, and returns-based analysis alone is not enough for every fund. Some styles cannot be identified easily by returns-based or holdings-based methods: the styles of equity hedge funds, equity income funds, and special sector funds can be more efficiently identified using a combination of manager self-identification and holdings- or returns-based analysis. Some equity hedge fund styles are non-standard and do not fit into any of the established style categories at all, including long/short equity, equity market neutral, and dedicated short bias, which is exactly where the manager's own description carries the most weight.
rationales.C: Equity strategy investment styles result from the active equity manager's employment of a particular strategy to manage the fund, and that strategy is usually described in the fund prospectus, which can be used to identify the fund's investment objective. That objective can be regarded as the manager's self-identification of the investment style. Returns-based or holdings-based style analysis is then commonly used to identify the investment style - such as value/growth or large cap/small cap - and to determine whether it corresponds to the manager's self-identified style. Some other styles cannot be identified easily by such methods: the styles of equity hedge funds, equity income funds, and special sector funds are more efficiently identified using a combination of manager self-identification and holdings- or returns-based analysis, and some equity hedge fund styles are non-standard and fit none of the established categories, such as long/short equity, equity market neutral, and dedicated short bias.
